Group 5 — Heart failure and Asia

Studio wall

Author

Group names here

Spine

Who dies after heart failure, who grew up poor in the GSS, and where in Asia is life short?

This sentence stays at the top. Every panel must attach to it. If a plot cannot be introduced in a clause that hangs off this line, it is off the wall.

Introduction — the tables we own

This folder is ours for the ten days. Three tables, three shapes.

  • Panel A (panel-A.csv) — heart-failure clinic file. 0/1 flags have been recoded to yes/no. Quants: age, ejection fraction, serum measures, time.
  • Panel B (panel-B.csv) — GSS 1974–2002: ethnicity, city at 16, low income at 16, immigrant, plus years of education (Quant).
  • Panel C (panel-C.csv) — gapminder 2007, Asia only. Stand-in for an NFHS / malaria map. India is one country row, not districts.

C is not a Bangalore street map. If we want feet-on-ground geography, that is a different brick (OSM), not this file.

We load from this folder:

1. See the table

What is a case? Which columns are Quant / Qual? What is missing?

# glimpse() / inspect() / skim()

2. Ask

One question this table can answer. One it cannot. Write both.

Possibly can answer:

  1. Who smokes more, male or female?
  2. How does the age distribution differ between patients who survived and patients who died?
  3. Is the blood pressure of people who die higer or lower than the people who live
  4. Do patients with anaemia die more often?
  5. Does sodium level in the blood differ between patients who survived and died?
  6. Is there a difference in heart-damage between diabetics and non-diabetics?
  7. Is High blood pressure affected by age?
  8. Does a weaker heart mean patients don’t survive as long?

Possibly cannot answer:

  1. Does getting older cause death in heart failure patients? (The data does not show that one causes the other)

  2. What happened to patients after the study ended? (we don’t know about later outcomes.)

6. Say

Patients who died were older on average (about 65 years) than those who survived (about 59). The difference of roughly 6.5 years is statistically significant (t = -4.19, p= 4.735e-05 (0.00004735), p < 0.001)

7. Limit

What this panel cannot do. Which kit table we refused to abuse.

We can see patterns in who died, but we cannot say what caused the deaths or whether these patterns apply to everyone with heart failure.

1. See the table

What is a case? Which columns are Quant / Qual? What is missing?

# glimpse() / inspect() / skim()

2. Ask

One question this table can answer. One it cannot. Write both.

Possibly can answer:

  1. Were immigrants more likely to grow up in a low-income family? Immigrants and low income at 16 (shown through education)
  2. Does education differ between people who grew up low-income and those who didn’t? Education and low income at 16
  3. Does growing up low-income relate to number of kids? (Main Character)
  4. Do people with more education have fewer kids?
  5. Do immigrants have a different number of kids?
  6. How many years of education do people have?

2. Ask

One question this table can answer. One it cannot. Write both.

Possibly can answer:

  1. Which continents have the highest GDP per capita?

  2. Which continents have the largest total populations?

  3. Does life expectancy vary across continents?

  4. How do countries around the world differ in life expectancy, population, and GDP per capita in 2007?

  5. Is higher GDP per capita associated with higher life expectancy?

  6. Do countries with larger populations tend to have lower life expectancy?

Possibly cannot answer:

  1. Has GDP per capita changed over the years?

  2. Has life expectancy improved over the years?

  3. Does having a higher GDP per capita cause people to live longer?

6. Say

Caption + one sentence we will stand behind. Title is a sentence, not a column name.

Life Expectancy

Sub-Saharan Africa trails the world in life expectancy

The dark purple cluster across central and southern Africa stands out starkly against the yellow-green of Europe, North America and Australia, where people live well into their 80s.

Population

China and India are in a population category of their own

China and India stand out as clear outliers, they burn so bright on the map, every other country fades into the dark.

GDP per capita

North America, Europe and Australia lead in GDP per capita while Africa and South Asia lag far behind

North America, Western Europe and Australia glow green against a largely dark purple map, with Africa and South Asia showing the lowest GDP per capita by a wide margin.

The pattern across all three maps tells the same story: the countries with the highest GDP per capita also live the longest.

7. Limit

What this panel cannot do. Which kit table we refused to abuse.

Russia, the USA and the Democratic Republic of Congo are missing from the map.

The USA and Russia are among the largest economies in the world, and the DRC is one of the most populous nations in Africa. Their presence could meaningfully shift the story these maps are telling.

Conclusion

What the spine looks like after three panels

Age, childhood income, and economic conditions show patterns in health, education, and life expectancy. However, these patterns do not tell the whole story.

What we will not claim

Correlation does not prove causation. Age alone does not explain heart failure deaths, childhood income is not the only factor influencing education, and higher GDP per capita does not automatically mean longer life expectancy.

Which lines were human, which were machine

Human: Choosing the questions, interpreting the graphs, and drawing conclusions.

Machine: Helping with code, debugging errors, and creating graphs and maps.

Limits

Panel A represents a specific group of heart failure patients. Panel B is limited by the variables and responses available in the dataset. Panel C uses data from 2007, and missing countries limit the map comparisons.

Overall, these panels show how data can reveal patterns, but we must interpret those patterns carefully and acknowledge what the data cannot explain.

# 1. Create the factory icon
factory_icon <- awesomeIcons(
  icon = "industry",
  library = "fa",
  markerColor = "red",
  iconColor = "white"
)

# 2. Build the interactive map
leaflet() %>%
  addTiles() %>%

  # Approximate groundwater contamination plume
  addPolygons(
    lng = c(
      -117.24, -117.22, -117.19, -117.16,
      -117.14, -117.15, -117.18, -117.21,
      -117.24
    ),
    lat = c(
      34.96, 34.97, 34.965, 34.95,
      34.93, 34.91, 34.90, 34.91,
      34.96
    ),
    fillColor = "blue",
    fillOpacity = 0.35,
    color = "darkblue",
    weight = 2,
    popup = "Approximate Groundwater Contamination Plume"
  ) %>%

  # Five families connected to the case
  addCircleMarkers(
    lng = c(
      -117.205, -117.215, -117.190,
      -117.225, -117.175
    ),
    lat = c(
      34.925, 34.940, 34.915,
      34.935, 34.945
    ),
    radius = 7,
    color = "darkgreen",
    fillColor = "green",
    fillOpacity = 0.9,
    weight = 2,
    popup = c(
      "Walker Family",
      "Harper Family",
      "Banks Family",
      "Park Family",
      "Killian Family"
    )
  ) %>%

  # PG&E gas compressor station
  addAwesomeMarkers(
  lng = -117.1622006,
  lat = 34.9035573,
  icon = factory_icon,
  popup = "PG&E Hinkley Gas Compressor Station"
) %>%

  # Center the map on Hinkley, California
  setView(
    lng = -117.20,
    lat = 34.93,
    zoom = 12
  )
